MlxIPC.Goal: MLXIPC is the message bus of MLX/brixOS (the service "synapse", projects/desktop/ipc) and its own wire format, the one the system's own programs speak (std.ipc). It carries method calls, replies, errors and signals between programs, with name ownership, routing and a permission policy. It is native first: our own programs speak this format; D-Bus (std.dbus) is a compatibility gateway at the edge for foreign software, not the default for us.
MlxIPC.Library: std.ipc implements the wire and a full client (connect, call, signal, reply, next); std.dbus implements the D-Bus wire and client. The two carry the same messages, so the bus translates between a native connection and a D-Bus one, and a native service answers a dbus-send caller.

Transport.brixOS: A channel pair (spec/04-stdlib/os/brix.xml, listener_make/node_open): messages of up to 1024 bytes carrying up to four handles each; the byte stream the wire expects is reassembled from them, handles arrive in order. A value of type h is a handle passed on the channel, not a byte in the body.
Transport.Linux: An AF_UNIX SOCK_STREAM socket; a value of type h is a Unix descriptor sent with SCM_RIGHTS.
Transport.Address: The bus listens at a listener node (brixOS) or a socket path/abstract name (Linux); a client finds it in DBUS_SESSION_BUS_ADDRESS or DBUS_SYSTEM_BUS_ADDRESS, as D-Bus clients do, so one address serves both formats.

Identity.Rule: A connection is authenticated by the transport, not by an exchange in the protocol. There is no SASL. The bus learns the peer's user and process from the channel or socket (brixOS: channel_peer, spec call 55, which also names the peer's program; Linux: SO_PEERCRED). A client sends no credentials and cannot claim another's.

The bus's permission policy (projects/desktop/ipc/policy.mlx) decides what an app may do by that identity: who the app is (its program's name on brixOS, else /proc on Linux), whether it is sandboxed, and the rules of the policy file. A service permission (for example login.session, audio.record) is asked for with Check; some are put to the user. Permission is a property of the connection's identity, established once by the transport, not carried per message.

Preamble.Bytes: 8 bytes each way: 'M' 'L' 'X' 'I', u8 version (1), u8 flags, u16 0.
Preamble.Rule: The client sends its preamble and its first message (Hello) together; the bus answers with its own preamble (the version and flags it agreed) and the reply, which carries the unique name. A D-Bus client's first byte is NUL, a native client's is 'M', so the bus tells the two apart by the first byte of the connection.

Header.Field: the whole message in bytes, at most 65536 (MAX_MESSAGE)
descriptors/handles sent with the message, at most 28
the call a REPLY or ERROR answers; 0 otherwise
bytes of the fields that follow the header

Message.Fields: Each field is a u8 code, a u16 length and that many bytes (no NUL, no padding). Each code appears at most once; a reader skips a code it does not know. The codes are D-Bus's: 1 PATH, 2 INTERFACE, 3 MEMBER, 4 ERROR_NAME, 6 DESTINATION, 7 SENDER, 8 SIGNATURE. The reply serial and the descriptor count are in the fixed header, not fields.
Message.Body: The values named by the SIGNATURE field, one after another, no padding.

Required.Kind: PATH, INTERFACE and MEMBER; no replySerial

Values.Rule: The signature alphabet is D-Bus's, so a signature means the same on both sides of the bus. Values are little-endian with no padding between them.
Values.Type: 1 byte, 0 or 1 (not 4 bytes as in D-Bus)
u32, the descriptor's index among the message's descriptors
u32 length, the bytes, a NUL
u8 length, the bytes, a NUL
u32 count of elements (not of bytes), then that many elements
a struct: the fields in order
a dict entry: the key, then the value
a variant: a signature (as g) of one complete type, then the value

DirectChannel.Rule: Two programs that will exchange many messages ask the bus once for a direct channel (org.mlx.IPC.Connect returns a handle of type h), then run std.ipc over it with attach() (no preamble, no Hello). A message then costs two hops instead of four. The channel carries handles, so a shared-memory descriptor (type h) moves over it and its bytes never pass through the bus.

Validation.Rule: What is read is checked as dbus-daemon checks D-Bus (std.dbus's validators): the header's reserved u16 is 0, kind is 1..4, serial is not 0, descriptors do not exceed the limit; each field appears once and is a well-formed name, path or signature; strings are UTF-8 without a NUL; booleans are 0 or 1; a variant holds one complete type; a descriptor index names one of the message's descriptors; nothing nests deeper than 32. parse() refuses a bad header, validMessage() a bad body, and the conversions refuse either. The bus drops a connection that sends one.

DBusBridge.Rule: The bus speaks D-Bus too (std.dbus): a D-Bus client authenticates with SASL EXTERNAL and the bus reads its credentials from the socket all the same. toDBus and fromDBus (std.ipc) carry a message between the formats, keeping the same fields and signatures, so a native service is called by dbus-send and a D-Bus service by a native program. A D-Bus body larger than MAX_MESSAGE once its padding is added cannot be carried.

D-Bus is for foreign software (desktop interoperability, MPRIS, and tools like dbus-send). The system's own programs speak the native format; the bus is where the two meet, not a reason for our programs to speak D-Bus.
